summary: Hemilä 2023 (38082300; 15 comparisons from 10 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials, regular oral vitamin C >=1 g/day in healthy children, adolescents and adults) found colds were 15% less severe (95% CI 9-21%), robust to excluding the three largest trials, with benefit on severe but not mild symptom duration. Credit is limited to cold severity within that scope (supported outcome common_cold_severity; no assumed primary-endpoint superiority; nutrition stays on the nutrition pathway); the Cochrane reviews (23440782, 17636648) were abstract-only and get no context.

applicability.studied_population: Children, adolescents and adults in good health taking regular oral vitamin C of at least 1 g/day, assessed for the severity of colds that occurred (15 comparisons from 10 RCTs).

identity.chemical_form: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid), oral, >=1 g/day regular supplementation; trial-specific tablets

population.description: 15 comparisons from 10 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials in people in good health at baseline: schoolchildren (mean age 9-12), adolescent swimmers, marine recruits and adults (mean age up to 44); colds per comparison 20-1279 (Table 1).

study_contexts.study_design: Meta-analysis (fixed-effect ratio of means) of placebo-controlled trials of regular oral vitamin C >=1 g/day that reported both total cold duration and a severity measure; all included trials randomized and double-blind.

outcomes.name: Common cold severity: vitamin C reduced severity by 15% (95% CI 9-21%) vs placebo across 15 comparisons; 19% (P=0.001) after excluding the three largest trials
Direct mild vs severe comparison (5 comparisons): significant benefit on duration of severe symptoms; no significant effect on duration of mild symptoms

limitations: Effect on colds occurring during regular supplementation in healthy people; not treatment started after symptom onset (therapeutic trials were few) and not prevention of cold incidence in the general population.
Analysis restricted to trials reporting both duration and severity; control-group contamination (vitamin C intake in placebo arms) in six comparisons may bias toward null.
Trials date mainly from 1961-1981 plus 1998 and 2011; >=1 g/day is the inclusion criterion, not a validated minimum. Nutritional adequacy and the UL are assessed separately.
Includes children and adolescents (age_group mixed); not specific to any disease population.
Returned decision A119: source-content hold; methods now verified from full text. Cochrane 23440782 and 17636648 full texts not retrievable; no contexts for them.
Some included-study citations lack PubMed identifiers in the source XML; retain their exact citations rather than inventing identifiers.

Historical bibliography census (not independent scoring sources; actual included-publication membership is separately bound to the inspected source table): 765514, 4601508, 5057006, 4684621, 897573, 20689965, 368370, 7048833, 318715. Each intervention and comparison requires its own applicability assessment; citation in this bibliography grants no credit.

Included-study identifiers are now bound to this source's actual included-study rows/explicit inclusion references (Tables Tab1 explicit included-study row citations), with live NIH title/content identity checks. They are publication pointers, not independent-cohort counts, per-primary-study scoring approvals, preparation equivalence or new efficacy evidence. Exact unindexed source citations remain retained; no missing PMID is invented.

3 included source citations have no printed PubMed identifier in this primary source; their exact citations are retained in the source-table receipt. This is a documented identifier limitation, not a fabricated identifier or an extra independent trial.

Dr. Pham's fourth ruling set (2026-10-28): clinical credit only for common-cold severity within this review's scope (15 comparisons, 10 RCTs); the review designates no primary endpoint, so no prespecified, multiplicity-controlled superiority is assumed. Nutritional vitamin C adequacy stays on the nutrition pathway.
Context authored and source-verified by agent review (Claude) on 2026-10-28; Dr. Pham's pre-approval of fully source-verified contexts attested by Sean on 2026-10-28.

dose.administration_frequency: Regular daily dosing; 1 g/day in 11 comparisons, 2 g/day in 2, and 1 g/day increased to 4 g/day for the first 3 days of colds in 2 (Results).
dosage_forms: oral vitamin C tablet (trial-specific; tablets named in contamination analysis)
dose.reported_regimen: Table 1/Results: 1 g/day (11 comparisons), 2 g/day (2), 1 g/day plus 3 g/day extra during the first 3 days of colds (2); trial durations 2-5 months, two about one week.

normalization.basis: No scalar pooled dose; per-comparison g/day retained (1 g = 1,000 mg).

integration_notes: 2026-10-28 integrator: condition gate kept (supported_outcomes ['common_cold_severity'] equals the context condition). Sean's decision is that a claim-free label may earn scoped condition credit, but today the population limits (e.g. men-only, pregnancy, children) are enforced only inside this gate, so ungating via data would drop those safeguards. Claim-free scoped credit waits for the shared applicability change (no claim / aligned claim / unrelated claim / population mismatch) under /pg-scoring-change.
